```{r setup}
library(arrow)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(stringr)
library(scales)
library(gt)
library(here)

options(arrow.skip_nul = TRUE)

OUTPUT_DIR    <- here("phase2", "output", "deliverable01")
TRIGGERS_PATH <- here("phase2", "data", "analysis", "deliverable01", "projects_nepa_trigger.parquet")
PROJECTS_PATH <- here("phase2", "data", "analysis", "projects_combined.parquet")

# Read only the scalar columns needed — explicitly excludes every Arrow list<string>
# column in both parquets (nepa_trigger_secondary, project_type, project_state,
# lead_agency_harmonized, etc.) so collect() returns a plain R tibble with no
# arrow_list vctrs columns that would break sum() / mean().
trigger_cols <- c(
  "project_id", "nepa_trigger_primary", "nepa_trigger_count", "nepa_trigger_combo",
  "nepa_trigger_confidence", "nepa_trigger_rule_id",
  "nepa_trigger_evidence_source", "nepa_trigger_manual_review", "is_dual_nexus"
)
# nepa_trigger_multi and nepa_trigger_secondary are list<string> Arrow types —
# excluded here; n_multi_label is derived from nepa_trigger_count instead.
project_cols <- c(
  "project_id", "project_energy_type", "process_type", "project_department"
)

triggers <- read_parquet(TRIGGERS_PATH, col_select = all_of(trigger_cols))
projects <- read_parquet(PROJECTS_PATH, col_select = all_of(project_cols))

df <- left_join(triggers, projects, by = "project_id") |>
  filter(project_energy_type == "Clean") |>
  collect()

n_total      <- nrow(df)
n_unknown    <- sum(df$nepa_trigger_primary == "unknown", na.rm = TRUE)
n_resolved   <- n_total - n_unknown
pct_resolved <- n_resolved / n_total * 100
pct_unknown  <- n_unknown  / n_total * 100

get_n <- function(cls) sum(df$nepa_trigger_primary == cls, na.rm = TRUE)

n_funding      <- get_n("federal_funding")
n_direct       <- get_n("federal_direct_action")
n_land         <- get_n("federal_land")
n_permit       <- get_n("federal_permit")
n_program      <- get_n("federal_program")
n_property     <- get_n("federal_property_transaction")
n_pma          <- get_n("pma")
n_dual_nexus   <- sum(df$is_dual_nexus,          na.rm = TRUE)
n_multi_label  <- sum(df$nepa_trigger_count > 1, na.rm = TRUE)
flag_rate      <- mean(df$nepa_trigger_manual_review, na.rm = TRUE)

# Multi-label overlap structure (recomputed from nepa_trigger_combo each render)
multi_combo   <- df$nepa_trigger_combo[df$nepa_trigger_count > 1]
n_pma_land    <- sum(str_detect(multi_combo, "pma") &
                     str_detect(multi_combo, "federal_land"), na.rm = TRUE)
n_multi_other <- n_multi_label - sum(str_detect(multi_combo, "pma"), na.rm = TRUE)

pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", x / n_total * 100)

# Tier-by-tier yield, derived from the rule_id prefix so the pipeline table always
# reflects the parquet actually on disk (unknowns are the T4 rows that failed all gates).
tier_key <- str_extract(df$nepa_trigger_rule_id, "^T[0-9]+[ab]?")
tier_n   <- function(key) sum(tier_key == key & df$nepa_trigger_primary != "unknown",
                              na.rm = TRUE)
n_t0  <- tier_n("T0");  n_t1a <- tier_n("T1a"); n_t1b <- tier_n("T1b")
n_t2  <- tier_n("T2");  n_t3  <- tier_n("T3");  n_t3b <- tier_n("T3b")
n_t4  <- tier_n("T4");  n_t5  <- tier_n("T5")
cum_t0  <- n_t0;            cum_t1a <- cum_t0  + n_t1a; cum_t1b <- cum_t1a + n_t1b
cum_t2  <- cum_t1b + n_t2;  cum_t3  <- cum_t2  + n_t3;  cum_t3b <- cum_t3  + n_t3b
cum_t4  <- cum_t3b + n_t4;  cum_t5  <- cum_t4  + n_t5

# Pre-computed analysis outputs
source_dist <- read_csv(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "trigger_source_distribution.csv"),
                        show_col_types = FALSE)
excerpts    <- read_csv(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "trigger_evidence_excerpts.csv"),
                        show_col_types = FALSE)

# Secondary-trigger + review-status cross-tabs (04_secondary_review_crosstabs.R)
secondary_combos    <- read_csv(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "secondary_top_combos.csv"),
                                show_col_types = FALSE)
ml_by_process       <- read_csv(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "secondary_multilabel_by_process.csv"),
                                show_col_types = FALSE)
ml_by_technology    <- read_csv(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "secondary_multilabel_by_technology.csv"),
                                show_col_types = FALSE)
trigger_tiering     <- read_csv(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "trigger_tiering_crosstab.csv"),
                                show_col_types = FALSE)
trigger_regime      <- read_csv(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "trigger_regime_crosstab.csv"),
                                show_col_types = FALSE)

# Derived scalars for prose (recomputed from the CSVs each render)
top_combo_label  <- secondary_combos$combo_label[1]
top_combo_n      <- secondary_combos$n[1]
top_combo_share  <- secondary_combos$pct_of_multi[1]
second_combo_label <- secondary_combos$combo_label[2]
second_combo_n     <- secondary_combos$n[2]
ml_eis_rate      <- ml_by_process$pct_multi[ml_by_process$process_type == "EIS"]
ml_ce_rate       <- ml_by_process$pct_multi[ml_by_process$process_type == "CE"]
ml_transmission_rate <- ml_by_technology$pct_multi[ml_by_technology$project_technology == "Transmission"]
tier_n_enriched  <- trigger_tiering$total |> sum()
tier_n_determined <- (trigger_tiering$Tiered + trigger_tiering$Standalone) |> sum()
tier_n_tiered    <- trigger_tiering$Tiered |> sum()
regime_n_universe <- trigger_regime$n_regime |> sum()

# Funding deep-dive figures are optional (require the funding sidecar to exist)
has_funding_figs <- file.exists(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig8_funding_mechanism_counts.png"))
large_finance_path <- file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "large_finance_mechanisms.csv")
has_large_finance_table <- file.exists(large_finance_path)
large_finance_amounts <- if (has_large_finance_table) {
  read_csv(large_finance_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
} else {
  tibble::tibble()
}
```

## Executive Summary

::: {.callout-note}
## Key Findings

- **Funding is the dominant NEPA trigger**, accounting for `r comma(n_funding)` projects
  (`r pct(n_funding)`). DOE's grant and loan guarantee portfolio is the single largest
  source of decarbonization NEPA reviews.
- **Land** is the second-largest class at `r comma(n_land)` projects (`r pct(n_land)`)—BLM
  and Forest Service right-of-way and special use permits for utility-scale renewables on
  public land.
- **PMA/TVA** is third at `r comma(n_pma)` projects (`r pct(n_pma)`)—the federal power
  marketing administrations (BPA, WAPA, SEPA, SWPA) and the Tennessee Valley Authority
  acting as project proponent for transmission and power infrastructure.
- **Direct Action** is fourth at `r comma(n_direct)` projects (`r pct(n_direct)`), driven
  overwhelmingly by DOE building, operating, and modifying its own facilities—national
  laboratories and site operations.
- **Review process profiles differ sharply by trigger**: Categorical Exclusions are dominated
  by Funding (DOE's CE authority for grants); Environmental Impact Statements skew toward
  Land and PMA/TVA; Environmental Assessments show the most balanced trigger mix.
- **Trigger class predicts regulatory intensity**: Funding projects are overwhelmingly CEs;
  Land and Permit generate proportionally more EAs and EISs—land disturbance and regulatory
  licensing carry heavier review burdens than financial assistance.
- **Technology patterns reflect nexus logic**: Transmission has the highest PMA/TVA share
  (BPA and WAPA build and maintain federal lines); Solar and Wind split between Land (BLM
  right-of-way) and Funding (DOE grants); CCS and Energy Storage skew toward Funding via DOE
  emerging technology programs.
:::

This report delivers:

> Reasons why NEPA was triggered (e.g., federal land, federal funding) for different types of projects.

---

# Methodology

## Trigger Definitions

NEPA applies whenever a federal nexus exists—but the *nature* of that nexus varies. We classify
each project into one of eight mutually exclusive primary trigger classes using a strict priority
ordering (highest to lowest). When evidence points to multiple classes, the higher-priority class
wins as the primary; lower-priority matches are retained as secondary triggers.

::: {tbl-colwidths="[15,85]"}
| Trigger | Federal Nexus |
|:-|:---|
| **Program** | A programmatic EIS, land-use plan, or rulemaking umbrella covers the action — the NEPA review is at the policy or program level |
| **Direct Action** | The federal agency *is* the proposer — building, operating, or managing the project (e.g., agency construction, national laboratory operations, military facilities) |
| **PMA/TVA** | A federal power marketing administration (BPA, WAPA, SEPA, SWPA) or the Tennessee Valley Authority is the acting agency — building, upgrading, or maintaining federal power and transmission infrastructure |
| **Property Transaction** | A land exchange, disposal, or conveyance of federal property is the triggering event |
| **Land** | A private or state actor seeks a right-of-way, special use permit, or lease on federal land (BLM, National Forest) |
| **Permit** | A federal license or permit issued by a regulatory body (FERC license, FAA authorization, Section 404 dredge-and-fill) is the primary nexus |
| **Funding** | Federal grant, loan guarantee, or financial assistance is the trigger (DOE loan program, IRA grant, Rural Energy for America Program) |
| **Unknown** | NEPA is confirmed but the trigger cannot be reliably identified from available text or metadata |
:::

All five classification tiers obey this priority ordering. Tiers 0–4 enforce it mechanically
(each rule detects a single class, and the ladder settles conflicts). Tier 5—the LLM
fallback—proposes both the classes and its own ranking; the pipeline reconciles that ranking
to the fixed hierarchy at ingest, so every published primary follows the ordering above. The
LLM's raw verdicts are preserved verbatim in a committed adjudication record
([`tier5_adjudication_record.csv`](../code/deliverable01/tier5_adjudication_record.csv)), and
the published Tier 5 classifications can be reproduced exactly—without any LLM call—by
running `03_rerun_tier5.py --from-record` against that record.

Secondary triggers are stored separately in the `nepa_trigger_secondary` field; `r comma(n_multi_label)` projects (`r pct(n_multi_label)`) have more than one trigger class detected. The overlap is dominated by a single structural pattern: `r comma(n_pma_land)` of these pair **PMA/TVA with federal land**—BPA and WAPA transmission and power infrastructure that also crosses BLM or National Forest land, so both the power-authority-proponent nexus and the federal-land nexus apply. The remaining `r comma(n_multi_other)` multi-class projects form a longer tail—most often federal land paired with a federal permit, or direct action paired with federal land—surfaced largely by the Tier 5 pass, which records a secondary trigger whenever its adjudication of a previously-uncertain project identifies a second nexus.

## Workflow

The approach spends effort where it is needed: cheap deterministic rules classify everything
they can, machine-learning models take the bulk that rules cannot reach, and a
carefully-audited LLM pass handles only the hardest residue — with every automated judgment
gated, logged, and reproducible.

## Classification Pipeline

Trigger classification runs in five tiers plus a manual-label seed. Each tier feeds into the
next; a project is finalized the moment it clears a tier's acceptance gate and is never
re-processed by later tiers. This preserves precision at each level while reserving compute-
intensive methods for the genuinely ambiguous cases.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pipeline-flow
#| fig-cap: !expr sprintf("Cumulative trigger resolution across the classification pipeline. Each project is finalized by the first tier whose acceptance gate it clears; the %s residual unknowns are flagged for manual review.", comma(n_unknown))
#| out-width: "95%"

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig12_pipeline_flow.png"))
```

::: {tbl-colwidths="[40,20,20,20]"}
| Tier | Projects | Resolved (cum.) | % of Universe |
|:---|--:|--:|--:|
| Tier 0 — Manual labels | `r comma(n_t0)` | `r comma(cum_t0)` | `r pct(cum_t0)` |
| Tier 1a — Agency metadata | `r comma(n_t1a)` | `r comma(cum_t1a)` | `r pct(cum_t1a)` |
| Tier 1b — Title + description | `r comma(n_t1b)` | `r comma(cum_t1b)` | `r pct(cum_t1b)` |
| Tier 2 — Document title scan | `r comma(n_t2)` | `r comma(cum_t2)` | `r pct(cum_t2)` |
| Tier 3 — Purpose-and-need | `r comma(n_t3)` | `r comma(cum_t3)` | `r pct(cum_t3)` |
| Tier 3b — SetFit (DOE CE) | `r comma(n_t3b)` | `r comma(cum_t3b)` | `r pct(cum_t3b)` |
| Tier 4 — NLI adjudication | `r comma(n_t4)` | `r comma(cum_t4)` | `r pct(cum_t4)` |
| Tier 5 — LLM fallback | `r comma(n_t5)` | `r comma(cum_t5)` | `r pct(cum_t5)` |
| — Unknown | `r comma(n_unknown)` | — | `r pct(n_unknown)` |
:::

**Total resolved: `r comma(n_resolved)` / `r comma(n_total)` (`r sprintf("%.1f%%", pct_resolved)`).**
Per-tier methods (rule sets, model configurations, acceptance gates) are documented in the
[architecture doc](../architecture/deliverables/deliverable01.md).

The pipeline is implemented in
[`phase2/code/deliverable01/01_extract_nepa_trigger.py`](../code/deliverable01/01_extract_nepa_trigger.py).
The full output schema is documented in
[`phase2/architecture/deliverables/deliverable01.md`](../architecture/deliverables/deliverable01.md).

## Evidence Sources

The table below shows how many projects were classified from each evidence source and at what
confidence level. Agency Metadata reflects Tier 1a deterministic mappings; Purpose and Need
and Project Description reflect document-level text extraction (Tiers 1b–3); Document Title
reflects Tier 2 document title scanning.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-source-dist
#| tbl-cap: "Trigger classification counts by evidence source and confidence level."

source_label_map <- c(
  agency_metadata  = "Agency Metadata",
  purpose_and_need = "Purpose and Need",
  description      = "Project Description",
  doc_title        = "Document Title",
  setfit_inference = "SetFit Inference",
  manual           = "Manual Label",
  document_text    = "Document Text"
)

source_wide <- source_dist |>
  mutate(nepa_trigger_evidence_source = recode(
    nepa_trigger_evidence_source, !!!source_label_map
  )) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = nepa_trigger_confidence,
              values_from = n,
              values_fill = 0) |>
  arrange(desc(rowSums(across(where(is.numeric))))) |>
  mutate(Total = rowSums(across(where(is.numeric))))

source_wide |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    nepa_trigger_evidence_source = "Evidence Source",
    high   = "High",
    medium = "Medium",
    low    = "Low",
    Total  = "Total"
  ) |>
  cols_width(
    nepa_trigger_evidence_source ~ pct(44),
    high                         ~ pct(14),
    medium                       ~ pct(14),
    low                          ~ pct(14),
    Total                        ~ pct(14)
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = where(is.numeric), decimals = 0, use_seps = TRUE) |>
  cols_align(align = "left",  columns = nepa_trigger_evidence_source) |>
  cols_align(align = "right", columns = where(is.numeric)) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Confidence Level", columns = c(high, medium, low)) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold", align = "left"),
            locations = cells_column_labels()) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = nepa_trigger_evidence_source)
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style    = cell_fill(color = "#f0f4fb"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = Total)
  ) |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(16), data_row.padding = px(10),
              column_labels.font.size = px(16), container.width = "100%",
              table.width = "100%", table.layout = "fixed")
```

Coverage rates, residual-unknown composition, confidence tiers, and the caveats that should
accompany any reuse of this data are collected on the
[Coverage & Limitations](../notes/deliverable01/coverage_limitations.html) page.

# Trigger Distribution Overview

@fig-trigger-counts shows the total number of decarbonization projects in each primary trigger
class. **Funding** is by far the largest class—DOE's vast grant and loan guarantee portfolio
generates more NEPA reviews than any other federal nexus. Land is second, reflecting
utility-scale renewables sited on BLM and National Forest lands under right-of-way or special
use permits. PMA/TVA is third—the federal power marketing administrations (BPA, WAPA) and
TVA building and operating transmission and generation infrastructure directly. Direct
Action is fourth, driven almost entirely by DOE actions at its own facilities—national
laboratories and site operations.

Permit, Program, and Property Transaction together account for
`r comma(n_permit + n_program + n_property)` projects (`r pct(n_permit + n_program + n_property)`)—
these are real but narrow categories of federal nexus.

```{r}
#| label: fig-trigger-counts
#| fig-cap: !expr sprintf("Primary NEPA trigger counts across %s decarbonization projects. Colors match the trigger legend used throughout this report.", comma(n_total))
#| out-width: "90%"

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig1_trigger_counts.png"))
```

# Trigger Type by Review Process

## How triggers distribute across CE, EA, and EIS

@fig-trigger-by-process shows what share of each review process is driven by each trigger class.
The three processes reveal strikingly different trigger profiles:

- **Categorical Exclusions** are dominated by Funding—DOE's clean energy grant and loan
  programs generate an enormous volume of low-complexity actions that qualify for CE-level review.
- **Environmental Assessments** show a more balanced mix: Land (BLM/USFS right-of-way grants
  for solar and wind) and PMA/TVA (federal transmission projects) each contribute
  meaningfully alongside Funding.
- **Environmental Impact Statements** skew heavily toward Land, PMA/TVA, and Permit—larger,
  more complex projects requiring full EIS review tend to be sited on public lands, be
  federally constructed transmission, or carry FERC licensing.
- Unknowns are now a small residual across all three processes (`r pct(n_unknown)` of the
  portfolio overall). The Tier 5 LLM pass resolved most of the previously-large EA and EIS
  uncertain pools; the unknowns that remain—still modestly more common in EAs and EISs than in
  CEs—are the long-document cases where neither Tier 4 nor the LLM found decisive trigger evidence.

```{r}
#| label: fig-trigger-by-process
#| fig-cap: !expr sprintf("Primary NEPA trigger type by review process across %s decarbonization projects. Percentage labels shown for segments > 5%%.", comma(n_total))
#| out-width: "90%"

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig2_trigger_by_process.png"))
```

## What review process does each trigger class use?

@fig-process-by-trigger inverts the view: for each trigger class, it shows the share of
projects that went through CE, EA, or EIS review. This reveals the *typical regulatory pathway*
associated with each nexus type.

- **Funding** is overwhelmingly resolved at the CE level—consistent with DOE's categorical
  exclusion authority for grants and financial assistance that don't individually require
  significant analysis.
- **Direct Action**, **Property Transaction**, and **PMA/TVA** are likewise overwhelmingly
  CE-level reviews, owing to the routine, transactional nature of these actions—facility
  maintenance, conveyances, and line upgrades that require less rigorous review.
- **Land, Program, and Permit** produce substantially more EAs and EISs per project than
  Funding, Direct Action, and Property Transaction, reflecting the environmental scrutiny
  attached to land disturbance, programming, and regulatory licensing.

```{r}
#| label: fig-process-by-trigger
#| fig-cap: "Share of CE, EA, and EIS reviews within each primary trigger class. Percentage labels shown for segments > 5%; right-side labels show total project counts."
#| out-width: "90%"

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig3_process_by_trigger.png"))
```

# Multi-Label Structure: Secondary Triggers

Every project receives one **primary** trigger — the highest-priority federal nexus the
hierarchy resolves — but `r comma(n_multi_label)` projects (`r pct(n_multi_label)`) carry at
least one **secondary** trigger, a second nexus the pipeline detected but ranked below the
primary. These secondary labels are stored in `nepa_trigger_secondary`; this section
cross-tabulates them to show which nexuses co-occur and where multi-label projects concentrate.

## Which trigger classes co-occur?

@fig-secondary-cooccurrence pairs each multi-label project's primary trigger (rows) against its
secondary trigger(s) (columns). The structure is overwhelmingly dominated by a single pattern.

```{r}
#| label: fig-secondary-cooccurrence
#| fig-cap: "Primary × secondary trigger co-occurrence among multi-label projects. Cell values count projects with that primary/secondary pairing; a project with two secondaries contributes to two cells."
#| out-width: "85%"

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig13_secondary_cooccurrence.png"))
```

`r sprintf("%s of the %s multi-label projects (%s)", comma(top_combo_n), comma(n_multi_label), scales::percent(top_combo_share, accuracy = 0.1))`
share the same combination — **`r top_combo_label`**: BPA and WAPA transmission and power
infrastructure that also crosses BLM or National Forest land, so the power-authority-proponent
nexus and the federal-land nexus both apply. Every other combination is a long tail; the
next-largest, `r second_combo_label` (`r comma(second_combo_n)` projects), is barely a twentieth
the size.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-secondary-combos
#| tbl-cap: "Dominant trigger combinations among multi-label projects. Share of multi-label denominates by the 1,559 projects with 2+ trigger classes; share of portfolio by all 20,725 decarbonization projects."

secondary_combos |>
  slice_head(n = 8) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    combo_label  = "Trigger Combination",
    n            = "Projects",
    pct_of_multi = "Share of Multi-Label",
    pct_of_all   = "Share of Portfolio"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = n, decimals = 0, use_seps = TRUE) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = c(pct_of_multi, pct_of_all), decimals = 1) |>
  cols_align(align = "left",  columns = combo_label) |>
  cols_align(align = "right", columns = c(n, pct_of_multi, pct_of_all)) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold", color = "white"),
            locations = cells_column_labels()) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_fill(color = "#012169"),
            locations = cells_column_labels()) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
            locations = cells_body(columns = combo_label)) |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(15), data_row.padding = px(8),
              container.width = "100%", table.width = "100%")
```

## Where do multi-label projects concentrate?

Multi-label projects are not spread evenly. @fig-secondary-rates shows the share carrying a
secondary trigger by review process and by energy technology.

```{r}
#| label: fig-secondary-rates
#| fig-cap: "Share of projects with 2+ trigger classes, by review process and by energy technology (technologies with n ≥ 50)."
#| out-width: "80%"

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig14_secondary_multilabel_rates.png"))
```

- **Multi-label rates rise with review depth.** EISs carry a secondary trigger
  `r sprintf("%s of the time (%s), against %s for CEs", scales::percent(ml_eis_rate, accuracy = 0.1), "EIS", scales::percent(ml_ce_rate, accuracy = 0.1))` —
  the larger, more complex projects that warrant a full EIS are precisely the ones likely to
  implicate more than one federal nexus.
- **Transmission dominates.** `r scales::percent(ml_transmission_rate, accuracy = 0.1)` of
  transmission projects are multi-label — more than double any other technology — reflecting
  the PMA/TVA-plus-federal-land pattern that drives the entire overlap. Offshore wind and
  hydropower follow at roughly 10%, both siting-heavy technologies that routinely touch a
  second nexus.

# Trigger Class × Review Status

The natural next question is how trigger class interacts with the *kind* of NEPA review a
project received. The **review-type** axis — CE vs. EA vs. EIS — is covered in
[Trigger Type by Review Process](#trigger-type-by-review-process) above. This section addresses
the **programmatic vs. tiered** dimension: whether a review stands alone or tiers from an
umbrella programmatic document.

::: {.callout-note title="Data source"}
A portfolio-wide programmatic/tiered classifier does **not** exist in Phase 2. D2's outputs
(significance determinations, regulatory regimes) do not carry a programmatic/tiered flag. The
only committed programmatic/tiered signal is D6's FONSI-enrichment `is_tiered` / `tiers_from`
field, which is populated for the FONSI-enriched subset. The cross-tab below uses that
(correct) source and is scoped accordingly; a full-portfolio tiering classifier remains
deferred (see [Coverage & Limitations](../notes/deliverable01/coverage_limitations.html)).
:::

## Programmatic tiering by trigger class

Among the `r comma(tier_n_enriched)` FONSI-enriched decarbonization projects, D6 makes an
explicit tiering determination for `r comma(tier_n_determined)`; `r comma(tier_n_tiered)` of
those tier from a programmatic document. @fig-trigger-tiering shows how those determinations
split across trigger classes.

```{r}
#| label: fig-trigger-tiering
#| fig-cap: "Trigger class × programmatic tiering status, D6 FONSI-enrichment subset. Only classes with ≥ 3 determined FONSIs shown; 'Tiered' = review tiers from an umbrella programmatic EIS/EA."
#| out-width: "80%"

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig15_trigger_tiering.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-trigger-tiering
#| tbl-cap: "Trigger class × programmatic tiering (D6 FONSI-enrichment subset). 'Determined' = Tiered + Standalone; the tiered share denominates by the determined count only."

trigger_tiering |>
  select(trigger_label, Tiered, Standalone, Undetermined, pct_tiered_of_determined) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    trigger_label            = "Trigger Class",
    Tiered                   = "Tiered",
    Standalone               = "Standalone",
    Undetermined             = "Undetermined",
    pct_tiered_of_determined = "Tiered Share (of determined)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(Tiered, Standalone, Undetermined), decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = pct_tiered_of_determined, decimals = 0) |>
  sub_missing(columns = pct_tiered_of_determined, missing_text = "—") |>
  cols_align(align = "left",  columns = trigger_label) |>
  cols_align(align = "right", columns = where(is.numeric)) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold", color = "white"),
            locations = cells_column_labels()) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_fill(color = "#012169"),
            locations = cells_column_labels()) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
            locations = cells_body(columns = trigger_label)) |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(15), data_row.padding = px(8),
              container.width = "100%", table.width = "100%")
```

**Land-nexus reviews are the ones that tier.** Land is both the most common determined class
(36 FONSIs) and the most frequently tiered — 23 of its 36 determined reviews tier from a
programmatic document, overwhelmingly BLM's vegetation-treatment and herbicide PEISs. PMA/TVA
and Funding follow. The pattern is intuitive: tiering is a public-lands management device, so
it concentrates in exactly the trigger classes tied to BLM and Forest Service land. This is a
FONSI-subset signal, not a portfolio rate, and should be read as directional.

## Regulatory review regime by trigger class

For portfolio-scale context, D2's `project_regime` output assigns each EA/EIS project a
regulatory regime keyed to the CEQ rule in force at its decision date. The table below
cross-tabulates trigger class against that regime for the `r comma(regime_n_universe)` EA/EIS
projects with a regime assignment. This is a *regulatory-vintage* axis, distinct from the
programmatic/tiered question above.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-trigger-regime
#| tbl-cap: "Trigger class × regulatory review regime (D2 project_regime; EA/EIS decision universe). 'Pre-2020 CEQ' and '2020–2025 CEQ rules' bin the decision-date regime; 'FRA overlay' counts projects whose review window overlaps the June 2023 Fiscal Responsibility Act amendments."

trigger_regime |>
  select(trigger_label, n_regime, n_pre_2020ceq, n_ceq_2020_25,
         n_period_unknown, n_fra_overlay) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    trigger_label    = "Trigger Class",
    n_regime         = "EA/EIS Projects",
    n_pre_2020ceq    = "Pre-2020 CEQ",
    n_ceq_2020_25    = "2020–2025 CEQ Rules",
    n_period_unknown = "Undated",
    n_fra_overlay    = "FRA Overlay"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = where(is.numeric), decimals = 0, use_seps = TRUE) |>
  cols_align(align = "left",  columns = trigger_label) |>
  cols_align(align = "right", columns = where(is.numeric)) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold", color = "white"),
            locations = cells_column_labels()) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_fill(color = "#012169"),
            locations = cells_column_labels()) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
            locations = cells_body(columns = trigger_label)) |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(14), data_row.padding = px(7),
              container.width = "100%", table.width = "100%")
```

Land and PMA/TVA supply the largest EA/EIS caseloads, and both skew toward the pre-2020 CEQ
regime — the bulk of these public-lands and transmission reviews predate the 2020–2025 rule
churn. Roughly a third of the regime universe is undated (no reliable decision date recovered),
so these counts are lower bounds on each vintage.

# Trigger Distribution by Federal Department

@fig-dept-heatmap shows trigger class distribution across federal departments—the parent cabinet
agencies that house the lead agency for each project. Using department rather than individual
agency names collapses the ~18+ distinct agencies into a legible set of ~8 entities.

The heatmap reads row by row: each row sums to 100%, showing how a given department's projects
are distributed across trigger classes. For example:

- **Department of Energy** projects are largely Funding—DOE's primary mechanism for
  decarbonization investment is grant and loan programs—with sizable PMA/TVA and Direct
  Action shares from the power marketing administrations housed within DOE and from DOE's
  own facility and laboratory actions.
- **Department of the Interior** (primarily BLM) projects skew toward Land, as expected
  given BLM's public land jurisdiction.
- **Department of Agriculture** (Forest Service) mirrors Interior but at smaller scale—
  National Forest special use permits for biomass, wind, and transmission lines.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dept-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "NEPA trigger distribution by federal parent department. Each row sums to 100%. Cell text: share of that department's decarbonization projects in each trigger class."
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig4_department_trigger_heatmap.png"))
```

# Trigger Distribution by Energy Technology

@fig-technology shows trigger mix across primary clean energy technology types, filtered to
technologies with at least 50 projects. Technology assignment uses the first matching
clean-energy NEPATEC tag per project (e.g., a project tagged Solar + Utilities is assigned
to Solar).

- **Solar** and **Wind (Onshore)** projects are driven mainly by Land and Funding—utility-scale
  renewables either sit on BLM land or receive DOE financial assistance.
- **Transmission** shows the highest PMA/TVA share, consistent with the Power Marketing
  Administrations (BPA, WAPA) building and maintaining federal transmission infrastructure.
- **Nuclear Technology** shows the highest Direct Action share—DOE national laboratory and
  site actions dominate this category.
- **Hydropower** shows a distinctive mix of PMA/TVA (federal hydropower and transmission
  operations) and Permit (FERC licensing for non-federal hydro) alongside Funding.
- **Carbon Capture & Storage** and **Energy Storage** skew toward Funding, reflecting DOE's
  active grant program for emerging technologies.

```{r}
#| label: fig-technology
#| fig-cap: "Primary NEPA trigger by energy technology type. Technologies with fewer than 50 projects excluded. Right-side labels show total project counts; technology label = first clean-energy NEPATEC tag per project."
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig5_trigger_by_technology.png"))
```

The figures below use a funding details sidecar produced by the funding mechanism extractor.

## Funding Mechanism Types

@fig-funding-mechanism breaks down Funding-primary projects by the *type* of federal financial

## Dollar Amount Coverage and Distribution

@fig-funding-coverage shows what share of Funding-primary projects have each dollar-amount field

@fig-funding-amounts complements the coverage view with the actual dollar distribution per

mechanisms, excludes classes with fewer than 10 extracted amounts, and top-codes large grant-scale

# Geographic Distribution

## State-Level Dominant Trigger

@fig-choropleth shows the *dominant* trigger class in each state — the trigger type with the most
projects in that state. The map captures broad regional patterns:

- **Funding** dominates most states, consistent with DOE's nationwide grant footprint.
- **Land** dominates in the intermountain West (Nevada, Utah, Wyoming, Montana,
  Arizona, and New Mexico)—states with high proportions of BLM land and active solar and wind development.
- **PMA/TVA** dominates states with significant federal power authority infrastructure—
  Washington and Oregon (BPA) and Colorado and Nebraska (WAPA).
- **Direct Action** dominates Idaho, West Virginia, and South Carolina—states anchored by
  DOE national laboratories and site operations (INL, NETL, Savannah River).

Note that dominant trigger is determined by project count, not by area or capacity. A state
where a single large BLM wind project is the only decarbonization project will appear as Land
even if a dozen smaller DOE-funded projects are present.

```{r}
#| label: fig-choropleth
#| fig-cap: "Dominant NEPA trigger by state — the trigger class with the most projects in each state. Grey = no decarbonization projects in NEPATEC 2.0. Alaska and Hawaii repositioned for display."
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig6_state_choropleth.png"))
```

## County-Level Dominant Trigger

@fig-county-choropleth disaggregates the state-level map to the county level, revealing more
fine-grained geographic patterns in trigger type. Counties are colored by the dominant trigger
class among all decarbonization projects located in that county.

- The Funding / Land boundary maps closely onto federal land ownership: counties spanning
  BLM or National Forest land (interior West) show Land as dominant; counties without
  substantial federal land show Funding.
- PMA/TVA clusters in counties with federal power authority infrastructure—Pacific
  Northwest corridors (BPA transmission), parts of the Midwest, and Southwest transmission hubs.
- Many rural counties host only one or two projects and are therefore colored by a single
  project's trigger type; interpret sparse interior counties with caution.

```{r}
#| label: fig-county-choropleth
#| fig-cap: "Dominant NEPA trigger by county — the trigger class with the most projects in each county. Counties with no NEPATEC 2.0 decarbonization projects shown in light grey. Alaska and Hawaii repositioned for display."
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig7_county_choropleth.png"))
```

# Representative Evidence Examples

@tbl-excerpts shows two high-confidence classification examples per trigger class, drawn from
high-quality evidence sources (Purpose and Need sections, project descriptions, and document
titles). These excerpts are selected to show visible trigger-specific language and are intended
to be quotable in client reports.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-excerpts
#| tbl-cap: "Representative evidence text by trigger class. Two high-confidence examples per class; source limited to Purpose and Need, Project Description, and Document Title. Excerpts are selected around trigger-specific cue language."

excerpts |>
  mutate(
    `Evidence Text` = paste0("“", `Evidence Text`, "”"),

    `Project Title`,

  cols_label(

  ) |>
  cols_width(

    `Lead Agency`     ~ px(130),
    `Project Title`   ~ px(160),
    `Evidence Text`   ~ px(600),
    `Evidence Source` ~ px(95)
  ) |>
  cols_align(align = "left") |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold", align = "left"),
            locations = cells_column_labels()) |>
  tab_style(
    style = list(

      cell_text(color = "white", weight = "bold", size = px(13))
    ),

  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style    = cell_fill(color = "#f8f9fa"),
    locations = cells_body(rows = seq(2, nrow(excerpts), by = 2))

  tab_options(table.font.size = px(12), data_row.padding = px(8),
              row_group.padding = px(6), table.width = "100%",
              container.width = "100%")
```

# Reproducibility

Every number and figure in this report is regenerated by committed code, run from the
repository root. The one **billable step** — the Tier 5 LLM fallback — never needs to be
repeated: its raw verdicts are frozen in a committed adjudication record, and the record
replay reproduces the published classifications exactly, with no API call.

``` bash
# 1. Full trigger classification, tiers 0–4 (deterministic*, no API key)
conda run -n nepa python phase2/code/deliverable01/01_extract_nepa_trigger.py

# 2. Tier 5 — EXACT replication of the published classifications from the
#    committed record (deterministic, no API key, no cost)
conda run -n nepa python phase2/code/deliverable01/03_rerun_tier5.py \
  --from-record phase2/code/deliverable01/tier5_adjudication_record.csv

#    (alternative: statistical replication by re-running the LLM live —
#     ~$2 at claude-haiku-4-5 pricing; results equivalent in aggregate
#     but not guaranteed row-for-row)
# conda run -n nepa python phase2/code/deliverable01/01_extract_nepa_trigger.py \
#   --use-llm --tier5-budget 25

# 3. Funding sidecar (deterministic; reads the trigger output)
conda run -n nepa python phase2/code/deliverable01/01_extract_nepa_trigger.py \
  --funding-details-only

# 4. Figures + report CSVs (base R, not the nepa env)
Rscript phase2/code/deliverable01/02_create_figures.R

# 4b. Secondary-trigger + review-status cross-tabs (base R; reads D2/D6 outputs)
Rscript phase2/code/deliverable01/04_secondary_review_crosstabs.R

# 5. This report
quarto render phase2/reports/deliverable01.qmd
```

^\*^ Tiers 0–3 are exactly deterministic. Tiers 3b/4 run neural inference on Apple MPS
without a pinned seed and can drift by a few borderline projects between machines or runs
(measured: 1 project between the May and July 2026 runs); any such project enters the Tier 5
queue, where the committed record pins its published classification. See the
[Coverage & Limitations](../notes/deliverable01/coverage_limitations.html) page and the
[architecture doc](../architecture/deliverables/deliverable01.md) for the full
reproducibility discussion.
